description: This hackathon aims to use NASA satellite data and modern technology to help Moroccan farmers make smarter agricultural decisions and adapt to climate change. Over 48 hours, participants from fields such as programming, satellite data analysis, agricultural science, and design will collaborate to develop innovative solutions for Moroccan agriculture.
summary:
TURBA — Giving Every Field a Smarter Future

A farmer's greatest challenge is not simply growing crops; it is making the right decisions when the future of the land becomes uncertain. When should the field be irrigated? How is the soil changing? What environmental conditions could affect the next harvest? These questions inspired TURBA.

We developed a global, coordinate-based agricultural decision-support platform that transforms environmental and satellite information into practical insights. Through an interactive map, users can explore farms, draw field boundaries, and access climate data from NASA POWER and Open-Meteo, soil estimates from ISRIC SoilGrids, and Sentinel-2 metadata through Copernicus. FAO-56-based calculations help estimate crop water requirements and support irrigation decisions.

TURBA brings these resources together to make agricultural information more accessible, encourage responsible water use, and support better land management.

Its importance goes beyond technology: farmers' livelihoods, food security, and environmental sustainability are deeply connected. By connecting scientific knowledge with farmers' experience, TURBA aims to help agriculture face climate uncertainty and build a more sustainable future.
details: TURBA — When the Sky Changes, Farmers Deserve a Wider View of the Earth For generations, farmers learned to read the sky. They watched the stars, followed the winds, observed the clouds, and recognized seasonal patterns to understand when rain might come and when it was time to plant. Their knowledge was built through generations of experience and a deep connection with the land. But today, the sky is changing. Climate patterns are becoming less predictable, rainfall is shifting, and traditional signs are no longer always enough. Behind this uncertainty are farmers, families, livelihoods, and entire communities whose futures depend on the land. This is why we created TURBA. TURBA is a coordinate-based agricultural decision-support platform that connects Earth observation, environmental data, soil information, and agricultural science to help farmers better understand their land and make more informed decisions. Through an interactive global map powered by Google Maps Platform, users can explore geographical locations, select their fields, and define agricultural boundaries. TURBA then combines information from several environmental sources: NASA POWER for historical and environmental climate parameters, including temperature, humidity, rainfall, solar radiation, wind, and soil-moisture-related indicators; Open-Meteo for weather forecasts and model-based environmental data; ISRIC SoilGrids for spatial estimates of soil properties; and the Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem to retrieve Sentinel-2 satellite imagery catalog information, including acquisition dates and cloud-cover metadata. What makes TURBA more than a data visualization platform is its agricultural calculation engine. It incorporates established scientific approaches, including the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith methodology for reference evapotranspiration (ET₀), crop coefficients (Kc), crop water requirements (ETc), and soil-water-balance calculations. It also considers available soil water, crop water depletion, and water-stress factors to support more informed irrigation decisions. Additional soil and rainfall calculations draw on established approaches such as Saxton and Rawls pedotransfer functions and the USDA Curve Number method. However, we believe that agriculture is about more than environmental measurements and calculations. Behind every field is a farmer whose income, family, and future depend on the decisions made every season. Water is not only a natural resource; it is also an economic responsibility. By supporting better-informed irrigation and resource-management decisions, TURBA aims to help farmers avoid unnecessary water use, manage limited resources more carefully, and strengthen the resilience of their livelihoods and communities. Our development team used TypeScript as the primary programming language, with React, HTML, CSS, Vite, Node.js, and Express.js to build the application and its services. We used Tailwind CSS for interface styling, Google Maps Platform for geographical interaction, and external environmental APIs and geospatial datasets to provide the information behind the platform. TURBA is primarily software-based and does not require specialized satellite hardware or agricultural sensors from its users. Our creativity lies in connecting two worlds: the traditional wisdom farmers have inherited from the land and the broader perspective offered by space technology. We also recognize the importance of understanding how soil and agricultural practices change over time, which forms part of our broader vision for more sustainable land management. Throughout development, we considered climate uncertainty, water scarcity, soil variability, scientific reliability, data accessibility, and the economic and social realities of farming. We also took care to distinguish between direct data retrieval, model-based estimates, and static reference datasets, rather than presenting every source as a direct measurement. We are not building technology to replace the farmer's wisdom. We are building technology to give that wisdom a wider view of the Earth. TURBA — Where Global Earth Observation Meets the Wisdom of Farmers, for a Smarter and More Sustainable Future.
